doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: 'Dance for Joy' and learning to orchestrate with Ray Wright
summary: After a Hartford Symphony premiere excerpt, Brubeck recounts his brother no longer orchestrating for him and Ray Wright guiding his first orchestral piece for Eastman.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. If we skip ahead to this piece, “Dance for Joy.”
Oh. Because that’s the only performance of that piece with the Hartford Symphony. That’s the premier of it. Yeah.
I’m wondering if in the time between “Elementals” and this piece, I would think your skill at orchestrating and arranging for a large ensemble has changed. Is that a fair statement?

Well I’ve learned a lot. I started with “Elementals” that was the first time. My brother informed me that he wasn’t going to do anymore orchestration for me and Ray Wright asked me to write this piece that we would do in Rochester at the Eastman School of Music. And I said I haven’t ever written anything for orchestra. And he said well I can hear in your music that your thinking is like a big orchestra. Well I had to agree with him because I do think sometimes with both hands full of notes.
I’m glad to hear you say that because sometimes when I listen to you play I feel like your two hands are like a big band.

Yeah. That’s right. So he said well you go ahead and write it and indicate what you think would be good orchestration. So I wrote the first movement, indicated the orchestration. And he came back to me and said your instincts are right and I’ll follow those indications, and why not on the next movement, you just orchestrate it. And if there’s anything that’s impossible I’ll tell you. And then he said no everything is possible. And then when we got to the third movement he said there’s going to be some French horn players remember you for a long time. But he said it is playable. And he got the best players in New York, studio players, all name guys. Because Ray Wright was well respected by all the musicians and he just could call them. For years he was the orchestrator and arranger at Radio City Music Hall so every week — not every week — but most weeks he’d have a new show, and it’d have to be ready to go, no mistakes, and just he was kind of perfect. And so he was a perfect guy to go to Rochester and teach at Eastman, teach orchestration, composition, and he was the perfect guy to get me going. It worked out wonderfully.
I think you called that a concerto for anyone who can afford an orchestra? Oh my. Yes there’s that one beautiful line in there, I think the French horns do [scats].
